subject: Vectorized function slower than its non vectorized version.

messages.author: 9860719641632b58
messages.subject: Vectorized function slower than its non vectorized version.
parts:
Hello, I hope this is not obvious. I am very new to STAN.

I have a user-defined function (convolution) and coded it twice, expecting the second, vectorized version to be faster. 
It turns out that it takes almost twice as long as the first version 1. Am I doing something wrong here?
I'm using pystan 2.4.0.1

Version 1 (not vectorized)
functions{
 vector convolution(int N, real tStep, vector aif, vector irf){ 
    vector<lower=0>[N] ctr; 
       for(i in 1:N){
           ctr[i] <- 0.0;
           for(j in 1:i){
               ctr[i] <- ctr[i] + aif[i - j + 1] * irf[j];
            }
         }
       return ctr*tStep;
 }



Version 2 (vectorized)
functions{
 vector convolution(int N, real tStep, vector aif, vector irf){
   vector<lower=0>[N] ctr;
   vector<lower=0>[N] summand;
   for(i in 1:N){
      summand <- rep_vector(0, N);
      for(j in 1:i){
         summand[j] <- aif[i - j + 1] * irf[j];
         }
      ctr[i] <- sum(summand);
      }
   return ctr*tStep;
 }


Cheers

Tammo

require(rstan)

model1 <- "

functions {
 vector convolution(int N, real tStep, vector aif, vector irf) {
   vector<lower=0>[N] ctr;
   for(i in 1:N) {
     vector<lower=0>[i] summand;
     for(j in 1:i) {
       summand[j] <- aif[i - j + 1] * irf[j];
     }

   }

 }
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
}
transformed data {
  vector [N] aif_;
  vector [N] irf_;
 
  aif_[1] <- 1;
  irf_[1] <- 1;
  
  for (i in 2:N) {
    aif_[i] <- 1 + aif_[i-1]*0.1 + irf_[i-1]*0.16;
    irf_[i] <- 1 + aif_[i-1]*0.06 + irf_[i-1]*0.13;

}
parameters {
  vector [N] beta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector [N] beta_t;
  beta_t <- convolution(N, 1.1, aif_, irf_);
}
model {
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
}"

model2 <- "

functions {
 vector convolution(int N, real tStep, vector aif, vector irf) {
    vector<lower=0>[N] ctr;
       for(i in 1:N) {
           ctr[i] <- 0.0;
           for(j in 1:i) {
               ctr[i] <- ctr[i] + aif[i - j + 1] * irf[j];
            }
       }
       return ctr*tStep;
 }
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
}
transformed data {
  vector [N] aif_;
  vector [N] irf_;
 
  aif_[1] <- 1;
  irf_[1] <- 1;
  
  for (i in 2:N) {
    aif_[i] <- 1 + aif_[i-1]*0.1 + irf_[i-1]*0.16;
    irf_[i] <- 1 + aif_[i-1]*0.06 + irf_[i-1]*0.13;
  }
}
parameters {
  vector [N] beta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector [N] beta_t;
  beta_t <- convolution(N, 1.1, aif_, irf_);
}
model {
  beta ~ normal(0, 1);
}"

cmodel1 <- stan_model(model_code=model1)

cmodel2 <- stan_model(model_code=model2)

fit1_n100 <- sampling(cmodel1, data=list(N=100), seed=10, refresh=1e5)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sum() slower than a <- a + ... in loop (was: Vectorized function slower than its non vectorized version.)
parts:
On Aug 8, 2014, at 4:58 PM, Marco Inacio <marcoig...@gmail.com> wrote:



> You're right! And for me it's more than just 10%:

Thanks for investigating. Two things surprise me about the model.

1. I'd expect the sum() version to be faster for larger N.

2. I'd expect a compilation failure because we don't allow
constraints on local variable declarations because there's no
good point to validate them. I'll investigate and open an issue,
but we shouldn't have constraints on local variables.

If aif were reversed (which could be done once or the data
structures could be changed), then you cold do this
with a slicing operation in one loop, reducing the body of
the function to:

vector[N] ctr;
for (n in 1:N)
ctr[n] <- sum(tail(aif_rev,n) .* head(irf,n));
return tStep * ctr;

But that'd probably be even less efficient as you're now
generating temporary lists for head and tail. Maybe we should
think more about expression templates, which would mitigate
the copying cost. I'm sure that's what's killing the sum-based
approach --- the allocations of the vectors, that is; but here
there's no way to reduce that cost because each summand is
a different size.

- Bob

P.S. I've tried to restrict the term "vectorized" to when
a function can take a vector for an argument as well as
a scalar, and that's not what's going on here. But it's
used all over in different ways in other packages and by
other people, so it's probably a hopeless battle to restrict
its technical meaning.

> vector convolution(int N, real tStep, vector aif, vector irf) {
> vector<lower=0>[N] ctr;

> for (i in 1:N) {
> vector<lower=0>[i] summand;
> for (j in 1:i) {

> summand[j] <- aif[i - j + 1] * irf[j];
> }
> ctr[i] <- sum(summand);
> }
> return ctr*tStep;
> }

> On Sunday, August 10, 2014 4:15:03 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> a function can take a vector for an argument as well as

> its technical meaning.
>
> Can we start calling such functions "vector friendly"? And some vector friendly functions are also "derivative accumulating"?

OK. And there are really two different ways to be "vector friendly".

1. the way log(vector) works, is componentwise. That is, it just
repeats log on each element.

2. the way normal_log(vector,...) works, which is to add the result
for each element together.

Eigen calls the former elementwise operations and the latter reductions.
Some reductions are built-in and not just accumulations over elementwise
definitions, such as sum() and maxCoeff().
> And a small number of for loops in Stan are "batched" by the compiler / processor?

I don't know what this means.

- Bob
